Sequential AIPE for the Standardized Mean Difference

Source: vignettes/seq-aipe-smd.Rmd
seq-aipe-smd.Rmd

The Research Question

An education researcher is evaluating whether a supplemental tutoring program improves achievement relative to standard instruction. The effect size is the standardized mean difference, δ = (μ1 − μ2) / σ, the difference between the two population means in units of the common standard deviation (Kelley, 2007; Kelley & Rausch, 2006). The researcher wants to report how large the effect is, with a confidence interval narrow enough to be informative. Designing a study around the width of the confidence interval, and not around the outcome of a significance test, is the accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) approach (Maxwell, Kelley, & Rausch, 2008).

Fixed sample size AIPE planning (DMAR::ss_aipe_smd()) requires a planning value for δ. When no defensible planning value exists, the sequential procedure of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018) applies: data are collected in stages, and a stopping rule decides when the confidence interval for δ is no wider than a target the researcher has chosen. The procedure is distribution free; it does not assume that the scores are normal.

The Method

With n observations in each group, δ is estimated by d = (M1 − M2) / sp, the difference between the sample means divided by the pooled standard deviation (Equation 24 of the article). The sampling variance of d is approximately the asymptotic variance divided by n. The asymptotic variance (xi squared in the article) depends on the two means, the common variance, and the third and fourth central moments of the two populations. The procedure estimates it from the data without assuming a distribution; the estimate is the row xi_squared of the result and is written V below. With width for the target full width (omega in the article) and z for the standard normal quantile of the confidence level, the procedure has three parts.

  • The pilot sample size is the larger of a minimum (m_0, 4 by default) and ceiling(2 * z / width) (Equation 21).
  • The stopping rule is met at the first n, at or after the pilot sample size, with n >= (4 * z^2 / width^2) * (V + 1 / n) (Equation 22). The term 1 / n is a correction that keeps the rule from being met too early.
  • The confidence interval runs from d - z * sqrt(V / n) to d + z * sqrt(V / n) (Equation 28). Whenever the rule is met its width is at most width.

Workflow

The researcher commits to a target full width of 0.50 at the 95% confidence level, computes the pilot sample size, collects the pilot sample, and checks the stopping rule. The data here are simulated from a population with δ = 0.50; in a real study each call to new_tutored() or new_standard() is a new group of students.

set.seed(113)
new_tutored <- function(n) rnorm(n, mean = 0.50, sd = 1)
new_standard <- function(n) rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)

m <- seq_aipe_smd_pilot(width = 0.50, conf_level = 0.95)
m
#> [1] 8

tutored <- new_tutored(m)
standard <- new_standard(m)
out <- seq_aipe_smd(tutored, standard, width = 0.50, conf_level = 0.95)
out
#> Sequential check (standardized mean difference)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 8
#>   Criterion n     : 134
#>   Target width    : 0.5
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : -0.8729387
#>   smd               : 0.1182492
#>   upper_limit       : 1.109437
#>   xi_squared        : 2.046001
#>   criterion_n       : 134
#>   current_n         : 8
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

The row criterion_n is the right side of the stopping rule, rounded up, and the limits are the interval described above. Both can be reproduced from the other rows:

z <- qnorm(1 - (1 - 0.95) / 2)
d <- out$value[out$term == "smd"]
V <- out$value[out$term == "xi_squared"]
n <- out$value[out$term == "current_n"]

ceiling(4 * z^2 / 0.50^2 * (V + 1 / n))
#> [1] 134
d + c(-1, 1) * z * sqrt(V / n)
#> [1] -0.8729387  1.1094371

The rule is not met at the pilot, so the study goes on: students are added to each group, five at a time here, and the rule is checked again after each addition, until it is met. vignette("step-by-step-sequential-workflow", package = "SMSD") writes that loop out. To show where it leads, the rest of the study is simulated here in one piece, 200 more students per group in the order in which they would have been recruited, and seq_path() applies the check at every stage the study would have reached.

tutored <- c(tutored, new_tutored(200))
standard <- c(standard, new_standard(200))

path <- seq_path(seq_aipe_smd, list(group_1 = tutored, group_2 = standard),
                 width = 0.50, conf_level = 0.95, by = 5)
path
#> Sequential path: standardized mean difference
#> 
#>   Stages checked  : 41 (n = 8 to 208 by 5)
#>   First check at  : the pilot sample size
#>   Target width    : 0.5
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Rule first met  : n = 128
#>   Estimate there  : smd = 0.4434397 [0.1946667, 0.6922126]
#> 
#>     n   estimate  lower_limit  upper_limit  criterion_n  is_satisfied
#>     8  0.1182492  -0.87293869    1.1094371          134         FALSE
#>    13  0.3174077  -0.48780686    1.1226223          140         FALSE
#>    18  0.5788349  -0.09901432    1.2566840          136         FALSE
#>   ...
#>   198  0.4355098   0.23537023    0.6356494          128          TRUE
#>   203  0.4102967   0.21259036    0.6080030          128          TRUE
#>   208  0.4115121   0.21716725    0.6058570          126          TRUE
#> 
#>   The estimate to report is the one at n = 128. Later rows show what
#>   the rule would have said had sampling continued; they are not grounds
#>   for choosing a different stopping point.
plot(path)

The rule was first met at 128 students per group, and that is where a study run as planned stops. The students simulated beyond that point are there only to complete the picture; they are drawn in gray in the plot, and an estimate from a later stage may not be reported in place of the one at the stopping point. At the stopping point the estimate is 0.443, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.195 to 0.692. The width, 0.498, is within the target, and the interval contains the population value of 0.50. The check at the stopping point is stored with the path as attr(path, "final_check"), and seq_report() writes the result up:

seq_report(path)
#> Sample size was determined with the sequential accuracy in parameter
#> estimation procedure for the standardized mean difference (Kelley,
#> Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018), with a target full width of 0.5 for the
#> 95% confidence interval. The stopping rule was evaluated from the pilot
#> sample size (n = 8 per group) onward, after every 5 additional
#> observations per group, and was first met at n = 128 per group. At that
#> sample size the estimate of the standardized mean difference was 0.443,
#> 95% CI [0.195, 0.692]. The confidence level is asymptotic; meeting the
#> width target does not establish nominal coverage at this sample size.
#> 
#> Reference
#> Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in
#>     parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A
#>     sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243.
#>     doi:10.1037/met0000127

The Correction to Equation 26

Equation 26 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, p. 232) gives the asymptotic variance of the standardized mean difference, and the sample version printed under their Equation 27 is what the stopping rule uses. As printed, both omit a factor of one half in the term that carries the third central moments. With μk3 and μk4 for the third and fourth central moments of group k, the printed equation is

asymptotic variance = 2 − (μ1 − μ2)(μ13 − μ23) / σ4 + [(μ1 − μ2)2 / (4 σ6)] [(μ14 + μ24) / 4 − σ4 / 2]

and the corrected equation, which the package implements, is

asymptotic variance = 2 − (μ1 − μ2)(μ13 − μ23) / (2 σ4) + [(μ1 − μ2)2 / (4 σ6)] [(μ14 + μ24) / 4 − σ4 / 2].

The two agree when the means are equal and when the two groups have the same third central moment, which includes every pair of symmetric distributions; for normal data both reduce to 2 + δ2 / 4. They differ when the means differ and the groups are skewed differently. The authors’ derivation of the corrected equation is posted at https://kenkelley.org/wp-content/uploads/articles/Kelley_Darku_Chattopadhyay_Equation_26.pdf, and the same document is installed with the package, at the path that system.file("eq26_correction.pdf", package = "SMSD") returns:

file.exists(system.file("eq26_correction.pdf", package = "SMSD"))
#> [1] TRUE

A case in which the two forms differ shows which one describes the data. Take two populations with unit variance and a standardized mean difference of 0.5, one right skewed (a standardized chi square distribution with 3 degrees of freedom, with skewness √(8/3) and kurtosis 7) and the other its mirror image. With unit variances the third and fourth central moments are the skewness and the kurtosis.

xi_squared <- function(delta, skew_1, skew_2, kurt_1, kurt_2, half) {
  2 - half * delta * (skew_1 - skew_2) +
    (delta^2 / 4) * ((kurt_1 + kurt_2) / 4 - 1 / 2)
}
skew <- sqrt(8 / 3)
printed <- xi_squared(0.5, skew, -skew, 7, 7, half = 1)
corrected <- xi_squared(0.5, skew, -skew, 7, 7, half = 1 / 2)
c(printed = printed, corrected = corrected)
#>   printed corrected 
#> 0.5545068 1.3710034

If the asymptotic variance divided by n is the sampling variance of d, then n times the variance of d across many samples should be close to the asymptotic variance. Four thousand samples of 200 per group:

set.seed(113)
n <- 200
reps <- 4000
row_var <- function(m) rowSums((m - rowMeans(m))^2) / (ncol(m) - 1)

x <- 0.5 + matrix((rchisq(reps * n, df = 3) - 3) / sqrt(6), nrow = reps)
y <- -matrix((rchisq(reps * n, df = 3) - 3) / sqrt(6), nrow = reps)
d <- (rowMeans(x) - rowMeans(y)) / sqrt((row_var(x) + row_var(y)) / 2)

n * var(d)
#> [1] 1.366181

The simulated value, 1.366 (Monte Carlo standard error about 0.031), agrees with the corrected form, 1.371, and not with the printed one, 0.555. The variance estimate that seq_aipe_smd() computes from a large sample of the same two populations is an estimate of the corrected quantity:

big_x <- 0.5 + (rchisq(50000, df = 3) - 3) / sqrt(6)
big_y <- -(rchisq(50000, df = 3) - 3) / sqrt(6)
big <- seq_aipe_smd(big_x, big_y, width = 0.10)
big$value[big$term == "xi_squared"]
#> [1] 1.368264

A reader who applies the printed equation to data like these would compute a criterion sample size less than half of what the corrected equation gives, and an interval too narrow by a factor of about 1.6.

When the Estimate Is Not Yet Usable

The variance estimate is a difference of terms built from sample moments, and in a very small sample that difference can come out zero or negative even though the quantity it estimates is positive. A check on such a sample looks like this. The scores are ratings from a pilot of five per group at a target width of 0.80.

rating_1 <- c(7, 6, 6, 7, 6)
rating_2 <- c(5, 3, 4, 5, 5)
early <- seq_aipe_smd(rating_1, rating_2, width = 0.80)
early
#> Sequential check (standardized mean difference)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 5
#>   Criterion n     : 6
#>   Target width    : 0.8
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : NA
#>   smd               : 2.696799
#>   upper_limit       : NA
#>   xi_squared        : 0.008
#>   criterion_n       : 6
#>   current_n         : 5
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE
#> 
#>   Note: The variance estimate is not yet usable at this sample size (it
#>         is zero, negative, or not finite), so the stopping rule is
#>         reported as not met. Collect more data and check again.
attr(early, "variance_unusable")
#> [1] TRUE

No variance has been estimated, so there is nothing from which to build an interval or a criterion. The check says so in four ways: the limits are NA; criterion_n is above current_n; the attribute variance_unusable is TRUE; and a note under the result says what happened. The stopping rule is reported as not met, so a loop written on attr(out, "is_satisfied") keeps sampling without any special handling. The row xi_squared shows the lower bound n−3 (here 5−3 = 0.008), not an estimate.

This is a deliberate departure from the stopping rule as printed. The article bounds the variance estimate below by n−3 (its Equation 27), and the printed rule would use that bound in place of a zero or negative estimate. The consequence is easy to compute for this sample:

z <- qnorm(0.975)
4 * z^2 / 0.80^2 * (5^-3 + 1 / 5)
#> [1] 4.993896
2 * z * sqrt(5^-3 / 5)
#> [1] 0.1567971

The right side of the rule is just under 5, so the rule would be met at once with 5 per group, and the interval would be 0.157 wide where 0.80 was requested: a study that stops at its pilot and reports a precision it does not have. The package uses the bound as the article prescribes whenever the estimate is positive, however small, and treats an estimate that is zero, negative, or not finite as what it is, no estimate yet. The same rule applies across the package’s check functions (see “An Unusable Variance Estimate” in help("SMSD-package")).

With more data the estimate becomes usable and the rule is evaluated in the ordinary way:

rating_1 <- c(rating_1, 5, 7, 6, 4, 6)
rating_2 <- c(rating_2, 4, 6, 3, 5, 4)
seq_aipe_smd(rating_1, rating_2, width = 0.80)
#> Sequential check (standardized mean difference)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 10
#>   Criterion n     : 82
#>   Target width    : 0.8
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 0.5535762
#>   smd               : 1.676233
#>   upper_limit       : 2.798889
#>   xi_squared        : 3.280935
#>   criterion_n       : 82
#>   current_n         : 10
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

For the standardized mean difference this situation is uncommon at the widths studies use. It arose above because the pilot was very small and the ratings take few distinct values. In the simulations of continuous data reported in ?seq_aipe_smd (a population value of 0.5, target widths of 0.4 and 0.2, normal and right skewed data) the variance estimate was never zero or negative, and at a width of 0.8 with normal data that happened in fewer than 1 study in 1,000 (?seq_aipe_sensitivity). It is common for some other effect sizes at wide targets, the correlation and the regression slope above all, and vignette("seq-aipe-correlations", package = "SMSD") gives the figures. A second, rarer case is reported the same way: when neither group shows any variation the estimate itself cannot be computed, and the check carries a note that says so.

What the Procedure Guarantees

The width is at most the target whenever the rule is met. That holds in every sample. The coverage of the interval approaches the confidence level as the target width narrows and the final sample grows (Theorem 4 of the article); it is an asymptotic property. How good the approximation is at a given width depends on the population value and on the distribution of the scores. In simulations of the procedure as shipped, with a population value of 0.5 and one observation per group added at each stage, 95% intervals contained the population value in 0.952 of studies at a target width of 0.4 (6,000 studies, about 200 per group at the end) and in 0.946 at a width of 0.2 (2,000 studies, about 790 per group) for normal data, and in 0.944 and 0.949 for right skewed data (?seq_aipe_smd). At a width of 0.8, where a study ends with about 51 per group, coverage was still 0.95 for normal data (?seq_aipe_sensitivity). For right skewed data at that width it is two to three hundredths lower. It is lower again at targets wider still, for normal data as well, and the more so the larger the population value.

seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity() runs the procedure many times for a population value, width, batch size, and distribution (normal or right skewed) of the user’s choosing, and reports the final sample size and the coverage to expect; vignette("sensitivity-analysis", package = "SMSD") describes its output and runs the skewed case just mentioned. When each observation has a price and the goal is the smallest total cost of sampling and estimation error, seq_mr_smd() is the procedure to use (vignette("mrpe-smd", package = "SMSD")).

Kelley, K., & Rausch, J. R. (2006). Sample size planning for the standardized mean difference: Accuracy in parameter estimation via narrow confidence intervals. Psychological Methods, 11(4), 363–385. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.11.4.363
